title: Ibrahim and Jamilah

full_text:
Ibrahim, a handsome and virtuous young gentleman of Cairo, saw an exquisitely painted portrait of Jamilah, daughter of the Grand Vizier of Basra, and his heart was stirred by her noble countenance.

Traveling across the deserts to Basra, he opened an art and book emporium near the city gardens. Jamilah, who was celebrated for her poetic learning, visited the shop to examine illuminated manuscripts.

Instead of declaring his passion with intrusive haste, Ibrahim presented her with an exquisite leather-bound volume of his own poetry, in which he had inscribed verses celebrating the beauty of virtue, the harmony of minds, and the sanctity of honorable companionship.

Jamilah read the poems with enraptured delight, recognizing a soul of equal refinement and moral elevation.

However, her father, intending to form a political alliance, had betrothed her to an arrogant general of the army.

With the assistance of a kind, venerable physician who recognized their pure devotion, Ibrahim and Jamilah presented their petition directly before the Sultan of Basra. Ibrahim recited a defense of sincere affection and family honor with such brilliant eloquence and poetic majesty that the Sultan was moved to tears.

The Sultan annulled the forced betrothal, compensated the general with an honorable military post, and celebrated the marriage of Ibrahim and Jamilah amidst thirty days of public festivities, proving that true eloquence and chivalry conquer the proudest barriers.
moral: Pure love, sustained by artistic eloquence and courteous chivalry, overcomes the widest distances.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Ibrahim and Jamilah"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
